reader.title: Shooting of a Black farm laborer and his son near Savannah (1905)
bases: A1 describes one white man shooting a Black worker and his son because the worker 'refused to work faster', set within the Tribune's complaint about white planters' treatment of farm hands; no mob or band is mentioned.
The only report is the Savannah Tribune's unattributed editorial aside (A1); no white-press or other Black-press account was found.

summary.text: The shooting of a Black farm laborer and his son near Savannah was an attack in the summer of 1905 in which a white man, in a county near Savannah, shot down a colored man and one of his sons after the man refused to work faster in the heat.
A second son escaped by running for his life, and the white man was not molested.
The case is known only from an editorial in the Savannah Tribune, which cited it as an example of the treatment that drove Black workers from the farms.
The Tribune raised the case while answering a New York Tribune piece, "The Negro's Passing Opportunity," reprinted in Alexander's Magazine for July.
In its view, one of the main reasons Black people left the rural districts was "ill treatment accorded them by a certain class of white planters, from which they have no redress whatever."
According to the Tribune, the shooting took place "in a nearby county some weeks ago," without a name, county or exact date.
A colored man refused to work faster "when the thermometer was near the century mark," and was cursed and "otherwise abused."
He and a son were then "shot down," while another son "had to run for his life."
The editorial does not say whether either of the wounded died.
The Tribune wrote that "the white man who committed the act was not molested," and no report of an arrest, inquest or trial was found.
The Savannah Tribune, a Black weekly, mentioned the shooting on 5 August 1905 as an aside within a notice recommending Alexander's Magazine.
It treated the case as typical rather than unique, calling it "one reason for the scarcity of farm helps in this section" and adding that "many more instances" could be cited.
The paper granted that many white farmers in the state were "humane in their treatment" and praised its "hundreds of prosperous colored farmers."
No account of the shooting was found in the white press for August and September 1905, and no other Black paper carried it in that period.

accounts.label: Savannah Tribune editorial
accounts.gist: In a nearby county some weeks earlier, a colored man who would not work faster in near-100-degree heat was cursed and abused, and he and a son were shot down while another son fled; the white man responsible was not molested.

framing.detail: The Tribune offered the shooting as proof that Black farm workers suffer 'the most heinous wrong' from 'a certain class of white planters' with 'no redress whatever', while granting that many white farmers in the state are 'humane'.

quotes: Because a colored man refused to work faster when the thermometer was near the century mark, he was cursed and otherwise abused, he and a son was shot down and another one had to run for his life.
The white man who committed the act was not molested. This is one reason for the scarcity of farm helps in this section.

One of the main reasons why so many of our people leave the farms and rural districts is because of ill treatment accorded them by a certain class of white planters, from which they have no redress whatever.
